results.name: new_set_first_trial_effect
results.description: Yes-rate on trials whose number_set differs from the set on the preceding trial_index (first query after a set change) minus yes-rate on trials repeating the previous trial's set; the model is history-free, so observed below null means people are more conservative right after a new set appears (and loosen with repeated queries), above null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: new_set_first_trial_effect
# description: Yes-rate on trials whose number_set differs from the set on the preceding trial_index (first query after a set change) minus yes-rate on trials repeating the previous trial's set; the model is history-free, so observed below null means people are more conservative right after a new set appears (and loosen with repeated queries), above null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    sets = df.groupby("trial_index")["number_set"].first().sort_index()
    prev = sets.shift(1)
    is_new = (sets != prev)
    flag = df["trial_index"].map(is_new).to_numpy(dtype=bool)
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    if flag.sum() == 0 or (~flag).sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[flag].mean() - r[~flag].mean())

results.name: narrow_span_outside_generalization
results.description: Among multi-example sets and targets outside the example range, yes-rate when the examples span <= 48 minus when they span > 48; observed below null means people generalise beyond tightly clustered examples less than the model's Erlang-width intervals imply (relative to spread sets), above null means more.
results.code:
# name: narrow_span_outside_generalization
# description: Among multi-example sets and targets outside the example range, yes-rate when the examples span <= 48 minus when they span > 48; observed below null means people generalise beyond tightly clustered examples less than the model's Erlang-width intervals imply (relative to spread sets), above null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1); hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    span = hi - lo
    outside = ((t < lo) | (t > hi)) & (n >= 2)
    a = outside & (span <= 48); b = outside & (span > 48)
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())

results.name: hull_advantage_by_set_size
results.description: (Yes-rate inside minus outside the example range) for 4-example sets minus the same contrast for 2-3-example sets, non-member targets only; observed below null means people's range-filling advantage does not grow (or shrinks) with more examples as the model's size-principle intervals predict, above null means it grows more.

results.name: round_target_penalty
results.description: Among sets with no example divisible by 10 and targets not in the set, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes-rate for other targets; observed below null means people avoid "round" targets more than the model (whose ends-in-0/multiples rules don't penalise them), above null means they favour them.
results.code:
# name: round_target_penalty
# description: Among sets with no example divisible by 10 and targets not in the set, yes-rate for targets that are multiples of 10 minus yes-rate for other targets; observed below null means people avoid "round" targets more than the model (whose ends-in-0/multiples rules don't penalise them), above null means they favour them.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    has10 = np.nansum((ex % 10 == 0) & ~np.isnan(ex), axis=1) > 0
    member = np.nansum(ex == t[:, None], axis=1) > 0
    keep = ~has10 & ~member
    rnd = keep & (t % 10 == 0)
    oth = keep & (t % 10 != 0)
    if rnd.sum() == 0 or oth.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[rnd].mean() - r[oth].mean())

results.name: inside_gap_width_effect
results.description: Among non-member targets strictly inside the range of 3-4-example sets, Pearson correlation between rating and the width of the gap (between consecutive sorted examples) that contains the target; under the model's intervals every inside target is covered equally, so observed below null means people fill wide gaps between examples less than narrow ones (local similarity), above null the reverse.
results.code:
# name: inside_gap_width_effect
# description: Among non-member targets strictly inside the range of 3-4-example sets, Pearson correlation between rating and the width of the gap (between consecutive sorted examples) that contains the target; under the model's intervals every inside target is covered equally, so observed below null means people fill wide gaps between examples less than narrow ones (local similarity), above null the reverse.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    n = np.sum(~np.isnan(ex), axis=1)
    s = np.sort(np.where(np.isnan(ex), np.inf, ex), axis=1)
    lo = s[:, 0]; hi = np.nanmax(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.nansum(ex == t[:, None], axis=1) > 0
    below = np.where(s <= t[:, None], s, -np.inf).max(axis=1)
    above = np.where(s >= t[:, None], s, np.inf).min(axis=1)
    keep = (n >= 3) & (t > lo) & (t < hi) & ~member
    if keep.sum() < 3:
        return 0.0
    g = (above - below)[keep]; y = r[keep]
    if np.std(g) == 0 or np.std(y) == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(np.corrcoef(g, y)[0, 1])

results.name: participant_parity_effect_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across participants (k-th row within each trial_index) of their parity-match effect (yes-rate for non-member targets with the same parity as the smallest example minus opposite parity); observed above null means people differ in how much they use parity/rule-based generalisation (individual strategy differences the single-parameter model lacks), below null means they are more homogeneous than sampling allows.
results.code:
# name: participant_parity_effect_sd
# description: Standard deviation across participants (k-th row within each trial_index) of their parity-match effect (yes-rate for non-member targets with the same parity as the smallest example minus opposite parity); observed above null means people differ in how much they use parity/rule-based generalisation (individual strategy differences the single-parameter model lacks), below null means they are more homogeneous than sampling allows.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    lo = np.nanmin(ex, axis=1)
    member = np.nansum(ex == t[:, None], axis=1) > 0
    same = (t % 2) == (lo % 2)
    pid = df.groupby("trial_index").cumcount().to_numpy()
    d = pd.DataFrame({"pid": pid, "same": same, "r": r})[~member]
    m = d.groupby(["pid", "same"])["r"].mean().unstack()
    if m.shape[0] < 2 or m.shape[1] < 2:
        return 0.0
    eff = (m[True] - m[False]).dropna()
    if len(eff) < 2:
        return 0.0
    return float(eff.std(ddof=1))

results.name: participant_yes_rate_sd
results.description: Standard deviation across participants (identified as the k-th row within each trial_index) of their overall yes-rate; the model has one shared parameter set, so observed above null means real individual differences in response bias, below null means participants are more alike than binomial sampling allows.

results.name: sparse_rule_far_generalization
results.description: Among non-member targets more than 15 from every example, yes-rate for targets belonging to a sparse rule (multiples of 6-12, squares, cubes, powers of 2-10; size <= 17) that contains all of a set's >=2 examples, minus yes-rate for far targets outside every such rule; observed below null means people extend sparse arithmetic rules to remote numbers less than the model's rule posterior predicts, above null means more.
results.code:
# name: sparse_rule_far_generalization
# description: Among non-member targets more than 15 from every example, yes-rate for targets belonging to a sparse rule (multiples of 6-12, squares, cubes, powers of 2-10; size <= 17) that contains all of a set's >=2 examples, minus yes-rate for far targets outside every such rule; observed below null means people extend sparse arithmetic rules to remote numbers less than the model's rule posterior predicts, above null means more.
def test_statistic(df):
    ex = df["number_set"].astype(str).str.split(",", expand=True).apply(pd.to_numeric).to_numpy(dtype=float)
    t = df["target"].astype(int).to_numpy()
    r = df["rating"].astype(float).to_numpy()
    valid = ~np.isnan(ex)
    n = valid.sum(axis=1)
    exi = np.where(valid, ex, 1).astype(int)
    member = np.nansum(ex == t[:, None], axis=1) > 0
    mind = np.nanmin(np.abs(ex - t[:, None]), axis=1)
    rules = [set(range(m, 101, m)) for m in range(6, 13)]
    rules.append({k * k for k in range(1, 11)})
    rules.append({k ** 3 for k in range(1, 5)})
    for b in range(2, 11):
        rules.append({b ** k for k in range(1, 8) if b ** k <= 100})
    in_rule = np.zeros(len(t), dtype=bool)
    for R in rules:
        mem = np.zeros(101, dtype=bool); mem[list(R)] = True
        all_in = np.all(mem[exi] | ~valid, axis=1) & (n >= 2)
        in_rule |= all_in & mem[t]
    far = (~member) & (mind > 15)
    a = far & in_rule; b = far & ~in_rule
    if a.sum() == 0 or b.sum() == 0:
        return 0.0
    return float(r[a].mean() - r[b].mean())
